subject: Banking
title: The ATM Revolution
description: A short lesson to help you apply The ATM Revolution.

hook.text: The first ATM opened in London in 1967. Barclays customers could withdraw £10 using a special paper voucher.

buildup.text: Before ATMs, you could only get cash during banking hours. If the bank was closed, you waited until Monday.

discovery.text: ATMs turned banking from a 9-to-5 service into a 24/7 utility. Cash became available anywhere, anytime.

twist.text: ATMs were supposed to replace tellers. Instead, banks opened more branches because ATMs made them cheaper to run.

climax.text: The ATM changed banking by making it invisible. Good infrastructure feels like it was always there.

punchline.text: First ATM: 1967, London, £10 limit. Banking became a 24/7 service.

quiz.question: What unexpected effect did ATMs have on bank branches?
options: Banks opened more branches because ATMs reduced operating costs

details.summary: The first ATM was installed in London in 1967, launching a revolution that gave bank customers 24-hour access to cash. ATMs transformed banking by enabling self-service transactions and beginning the long decline of the physical bank teller.
details.whyItMatters: ATMs were the first step in separating banking from banker. They proved that customers would gladly use machines for routine transactions, setting the stage for online and mobile banking decades later.
takeaways: Barclays installed the first ATM in Enfield, London in 1967
There are over 3 million ATMs worldwide today
ATMs eliminated most routine teller transactions and enabled 24-hour banking

faq.question: Did ATMs eliminate bank teller jobs?
faq.answer: ATMs reduced the number of tellers needed per branch but actually increased the total number of branches initially because they made branches cheaper to operate. Only the later mobile banking revolution began seriously reducing both tellers and branches.

faq.question: Are ATMs becoming obsolete in the digital age?
faq.answer: ATM networks are shrinking in countries with advanced digital payment systems like Sweden and China. However, ATMs remain essential for cash-dependent economies, rural areas without reliable internet, and populations without smartphones.
